system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2163-11-16 23:04:00 to 2163-11-19 17:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with a history of coronary artery disease, systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and chronic foot ulcers from prior frostbite, was admitted for worsening left foot pain, swelling, and erythema despite two weeks of oral antibiotics. Imaging revealed osteomyelitis in the fourth and fifth toes, and he was admitted for IV antibiotic therapy and source control. He underwent podiatric debridement of the affected toes, and a PICC line was placed to complete a 14-day course of IV vancomycin and ciprofloxacin. His pain was managed with scheduled and breakthrough opioids, with plans to taper upon improvement. His cardiac medications were held initially due to hypotension but were restarted before discharge. He was transitioned to extended care for antibiotic completion and was discharged in stable condition with follow-up arranged in podiatry, cardiology, and primary care.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of toe, unspecified
Ulcer of other part of foot
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my left foot’s been hurting more than usual, and I’ve been having a hard time catching my breath. I’ve been coughing too, and it feels like my chest is tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned shortness of breath—has it been worse when lying down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been sleeping propped up. It’s been hard to breathe flat. And my heart’s been racing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you had two toes amputated last month due to frostbite. Is the foot pain in the same area?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same foot, yeah. The toes look dusky, and I’m worried it might be frostbite again. I’ve been living on the streets, so it’s cold at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve checked an X-ray of your foot, and there’s no sign of bone damage or infection. Podiatry also looked at it and said it’s not active osteomyelitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? But it still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of infection, but we’ll manage your pain with oxycodone as needed. The bigger issue right now is your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows new opacities, and your proBNP is very high. That suggests your heart failure is flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart failure? I haven’t been taking my torsemide. I couldn’t get the prescription filled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely why you’re having more trouble breathing. We’ve restarted your torsemide and gave you IV lasix to help remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I did gain some weight lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep giving you IV lasix a few times a day. We’re also treating you for a COPD flare-up with antibiotics and steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: COPD? I’ve been wheezing a lot. Is that from the cold air?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cold air can trigger it, but your white blood cell count went up, and you have a cough with sputum. So we’re treating it as a flare-up with levofloxacin and prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I’m not as short of breath, but I still feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Your breathing sounds are improving. We’ll keep the IV lasix going and monitor your fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heart? I’ve been feeling palpitations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in atrial fibrillation, which you already have, but your rate is controlled. We’re continuing your rivaroxaban and carvedilol to prevent clots and manage your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been trying to quit smoking. I’m on the patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep supporting that. Your nicotine patch is still ordered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk about something that happened yesterday. You had a syncopal episode while straining on the toilet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt dizzy and almost passed out. I didn’t hit my head, did I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did strike your head. We did a CT scan, and there’s no bleeding in the brain. But there is a scalp hematoma, and we noticed a small mass that’s been slowly growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A mass? Is it cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. It’s not urgent, but we recommend a follow-up CT in six months to monitor it. For now, no treatment is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. That’s a lot to take in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. The good news is your breathing is much better, and your heart failure is improving. We’re switching you to oral lasix today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure your breathing stays stable and your medications are set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve spoken with social work. They’ve helped you get a place to stay with your sister, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, she’s picking me up. I’m really grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’ve given you a full month’s supply of all your medications so you won’t miss any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge help. Last time I ended up back here because I couldn’t afford the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the levofloxacin and prednisone for three more days. Keep using your inhalers. Watch for fever, worsening cough, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled follow-ups with your primary care doctor and podiatry. And don’t forget the CT scan in six months for the scalp mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doc. I’ll try to stay on top of everything this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call us if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a homeless man with a history of systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, COPD, and recent toe amputations due to frostbite, was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and left foot pain. He had not taken his torsemide due to lack of access, leading to an acute exacerbation of heart failure, confirmed by elevated proBNP and clinical findings. He also had symptoms and lab findings consistent with a COPD exacerbation, treated with levofloxacin and prednisone. A syncopal event occurred during hospitalization, resulting in a head strike; CT showed a scalp hematoma but no intracranial bleed, with incidental note of a slowly growing scalp mass requiring follow-up imaging. Podiatry found no active foot infection. Social work assisted with housing and medication access. He improved with diuresis and respiratory treatment, was discharged home with a month’s medication supply, and follow-up arranged for primary care, podiatry, and imaging.
